clip_narrations: In eighteen forty-eight in Vermont, Phineas Gage tamped black powder into a rock with an iron rod. A spark hit the stone and set off the blast.
It flew in under his left cheekbone and out the top of his skull. Yet minutes later Gage was talking, riding into town in an ox cart.
Within months his body healed, and he asked for his old foreman job back. His bosses said no. His friends said he was no longer Gage.
The rod tore through the judgment center behind his left eye, the spot that links feelings to choices. For his brain, this was a total nightmare.
Instead of staying wild forever, as many textbooks claim, Gage later drove a stagecoach in Chile. He steered six horses down steep roads for years.
First, picture the judgment center behind your eyes. It tags every choice with a gut feeling, like a quick warning before you say something rude.
Next, those warnings travel on wiring from the emotional alarm deep in the brain. The rod cut many of those cables on his left side.
Finally, strict daily routines in Chile helped healthy pathways in the front of the brain take over. That let him plan routes and steer six horses.
At Harvard, skull scans showed the rod cut about one tenth of the left frontal wiring. The researchers were left completely stunned.
Which is why the judgment center behind your eyes shapes who you are. And why even a badly hurt brain can learn to steer again.
